Hong Kong Metals & Mining Strike Halts Operations, Disrupts Supply Chain

A strike by hundreds of workers in Hong Kong's metals and mining industry has entered its third day, causing significant disruptions across the sector and prompting concerns from both industry leaders and analysts. The action, which began early Monday morning, has impacted several major sites, including facilities operated by MMG Ltd and Golden Peak Resources.

Workers, represented by the Hong Kong Industrial Metals Union, are demanding improved safety conditions, a 12% wage increase, and enhanced health benefits. "Over the past year, we have seen profits rise, but our members' concerns about workplace safety and fair compensation have not been addressed," said union spokesperson Lee Wai-ming at a press briefing outside the Central District offices on Tuesday.

MMG Ltd confirmed that its Tsing Yi processing facility has temporarily ceased operations due to the walkout. "We respect our employees' right to voice their concerns, and we are committed to engaging in constructive dialogue to resolve the current situation," an MMG Ltd representative stated. The company did not provide an estimate for when the facility might resume normal activity.

Industry sources estimate that the strike has idled approximately 60% of Hong Kong's metals processing capacity, with daily shipments of refined copper, aluminum, and steel down by as much as 45%. "The immediate impact is a sharp reduction in output, which will likely create a ripple effect across the regional supply chain if the strike continues," said Rachel Tsang, senior analyst at Asia Metals Insight.

According to the Hong Kong Mining and Metals Association, inventories at several plants are nearing critical lows. "If this disruption lasts more than a week, we may see contract delays and penalties start to accumulate," warned Association chairperson Joseph Chan.

Negotiations between union representatives and company officials have yet to yield a breakthrough. The Labour Department has offered to mediate, but as of Wednesday afternoon, talks remain at an impasse.

With no resolution in sight, industry participants are monitoring the situation closely, preparing for further supply shortages and logistical challenges in the days ahead. The union has indicated that workers will remain off the job until their demands are addressed.
